title: Cambridge Mathematics Extension 1 Year 11 — Chapter 9: Exponential and logarithmic functions

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a stated growth factor over successive decades and compare successive population values with a threshold.

inlines.text: Do not use a calculator in this exercise, except for the very last question.
The town of Goldhope had a small population in 1970, but the population has been increasing by a factor of 3 every decade since then.

children.label: a
children.prompt: By what factor had the population increased from its 1970 value in 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020?

answer.worked:
Each decade contributes another factor of $3$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{1980 factor}&=3^1=3\\\text{1990 factor}&=3^2=9\\\text{2000 factor}&=3^3=27\\\text{2010 factor}&=3^4=81\\\text{2020 factor}&=3^5=243\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the town’s population was $10\,000$ in 1970, during which decade did the population pass $1\,000\,000$?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Population in 2010}&=10\,000\times3^4=810\,000\\\text{Population in 2020}&=10\,000\times3^5=2\,430\,000\end{align*}$$
Since $810\,000<1\,000\,000<2\,430\,000$, the population passed $1\,000\,000$ during 2010–2020.

classification.difficultyReason: Generate powers by repeated multiplication, then select powers of related bases from a reference list.

content.prompt: Preparation: The answers to this question will be needed for all the exercises in this chapter. Keep the results in a place where you can refer to them easily.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write down all the powers of $2$ from $2^0=1$ to $2^{12}=4096$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: In the same way, write down:

answer.worked:
Start with $5^0=1$ and multiply each value by $5$.
$$\begin{aligned}5^0&=1,&5^1&=5,\\5^2&=25,&5^3&=125,\\5^4&=625,&5^5&=3125.\end{aligned}$$

Start with $6^0=1$ and multiply each value by $6$.
$$\begin{aligned}6^0&=1,&6^1&=6,\\6^2&=36,&6^3&=216.\end{aligned}$$

Start with $7^0=1$ and multiply each value by $7$.
$$\begin{aligned}7^0&=1,&7^1&=7,\\7^2&=49,&7^3&=343.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: From your list of powers of $2$, read off:

answer.worked:
Since $8=2^3$, select every third power of $2$, starting with $2^0$.
$$\begin{aligned}8^0&=1,&8^1&=8,\\8^2&=64,&8^3&=512,\\8^4&=4096.\end{aligned}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Combine rectangular-prism volume, cubed metric conversion and division by the volume of one grain to estimate a very large count.

content.prompt: A huge desert rock is entirely made up of coarse grains of sandstone, each about $1\text{ mm}^3$ in size, and is very roughly a rectangular block $3\text{ km}$ long, $2\text{ km}$ wide, and $500\text{ m}$ high.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the approximate volume of the rock in cubic kilometres.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many cubic millimetres are in a cubic kilometre? Answer in index notation.

answer.worked:
$1\text{ km}=10^3\times10^3\text{ mm}=10^6\text{ mm}$.
$$\begin{align*}1\text{ km}^3&=(10^6)^3\text{ mm}^3\\1\text{ km}^3&=10^{18}\text{ mm}^3\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the approximate number of grains of sandstone in the rock.

answer.worked:
The rock has approximate volume $3\times10^{18}\text{ mm}^3$, and each grain occupies about $1\text{ mm}^3$.
$$\begin{align*}N&\approx\frac{3\times10^{18}}{1}\\N&\approx3\times10^{18}\text{ grains}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use positive powers as repeated multiplication and the power-of-a-power law to cube the metric conversion factor. Calculate rectangular-prism volume in consistent units, then divide by the volume of one grain. The exercise instruction prohibits calculator use for question 9.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed step combines a cubed conversion factor with a large-number count, so calculations-scientific-notation is the closest catalogue match. Rectangular-prism volume and cubic-unit conversion support the calculation.

answer.short: Since $12=2^2\times3$, apply the power-of-a-product law, then multiply the indices in $(2^2)^n$.
answer.worked:
Since $12=2^2\times3$, raise each prime factor to the power $n$ and multiply the indices of a power raised to a power.
$$\begin{align*}12^n&=(2^2\times3)^n\\12^n&=(2^2)^n\times3^n\\12^n&=2^{2n}\times3^n\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: The mass of a neutron is about $1.675\times10^{-27}$ kg. About how many neutrons are there in 1 kg of neutrons?

children.label: b
children.prompt: The radius of a neutron is about $1.11\times10^{-15}$ m. Use the formula for the volume of a sphere $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ to find its approximate volume.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use the formula $\text{density}=\dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$ to find its approximate density in kg/m³.

answer.worked:
Use the unrounded volume from part b.
$$\begin{align*}\rho&=\frac{1.675\times10^{-27}}{\frac{4}{3}\pi(1.11\times10^{-15})^3}\\\rho&=\frac{1.675}{\frac{4}{3}\pi(1.11)^3}\times10^{18}\\\rho&\approx2.9\times10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Since $9=3^2$ and distinct powers of $3$ have distinct values, $3x-1=2$, giving $x=1$.
answer.worked:
Since $9=3^2$ and the function $3^t$ is strictly increasing, equal powers of $3$ have equal indices.
$$\begin{align*}3^{3x-1}&=3^2\\3x-1&=2\\3x&=3\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Solve simultaneously:

answer.worked:
Since $49=7^2$ and $128=2^7$, equating indices gives
$$\begin{align*}2x-y&=2\\x+y&=7.\end{align*}$$
Adding the equations:
$$\begin{align*}3x&=9\\x&=3\\3+y&=7\\y&=4.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}8^x\div4^y&=2^{3x}\div2^{2y}\\8^x\div4^y&=2^{3x-2y}.\end{align*}$$
Since $4=2^2$ and $\frac{1}{11}=11^{-1}$, equating indices gives
$$\begin{align*}3x-2y&=2\\y-x&=-1\\y&=x-1.\end{align*}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{align*}3x-2(x-1)&=2\\x+2&=2\\x&=0\\y&=-1.\end{align*}$$

Since $1=13^0$ and $25=5^2$,
$$\begin{align*}x+4y&=0\\5^{2x+10y}&=5^1\\2x+10y&=1\\x+5y&=\frac{1}{2}.\end{align*}$$
Subtracting the first linear equation from the last:
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{1}{2}\\x+4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)&=0\\x+2&=0\\x&=-2.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Find (and check on the calculator) the smallest whole numbers $m$ and $n$ for which:

answer.short:
$m=11$, $n=3$.

Compare integer powers for successive positive values of $n$.
answer.worked:
For $n>0$, the required inequality is equivalent to $12^n<2^m<13^n$.

For $n=1$, consecutive powers of $2$ bracket the entire interval: $2^3=8<12<13<16=2^4$.

For $n=2$, $2^7=128<144<169<256=2^8$, so there is again no possible $m$.

For $n=3$:
$$\begin{align*}12^3&=1728\\2^{11}&=2048\\13^3&=2197\end{align*}$$
Thus $1728<2048<2197$, giving $m=11$ and $n=3$. Larger $n$ requires larger $m$, so these are the smallest values.

Calculator check, to 2 decimal places: $2^{11/3}\approx12.70$, which lies between $12$ and $13$.

answer.short:
$m=15$, $n=4$.

Compare integer powers for successive positive values of $n$.
answer.worked:
For $n>0$, the required inequality is equivalent to $13^n<2^m<14^n$.

For $n=1$, $2^3=8<13<14<16=2^4$.

For $n=2$, $2^7=128<169<196<256=2^8$.

For $n=3$, $2^{11}=2048<2197<2744<4096=2^{12}$.

In each case, consecutive powers of $2$ bracket the entire interval, so no integer $m$ works.

For $n=4$:
$$\begin{align*}13^4&=28561\\2^{15}&=32768\\14^4&=38416\end{align*}$$
Thus $28561<32768<38416$, giving $m=15$ and $n=4$. Larger $n$ requires larger $m$, so these are the smallest values.

Calculator check, to 2 decimal places: $2^{15/4}\approx13.45$, which lies between $13$ and $14$.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect two constant-function limits with incompatible extensions of the index laws at zero, and explain why they do not determine a consistent value for zero to the zero power.

content.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0^+}0^x$ and $\lim_{x\to0}x^0$. Explain what these two limits have to do with the remark made in the notes that $0^0$ is undefined.

answer.short:
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^+}0^x=0$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}x^0=1$.

The different limits give conflicting extensions at zero, supporting the convention that $0^0$ is undefined here.
answer.worked:
For every $x>0$, $0^x=0$. For every $x\ne0$, $x^0=1$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\lim_{x\to0^+}0^x&=0,\\\lim_{x\to0}x^0&=1.\end{align*}$$
Extending the first rule to $x=0$ suggests $0^0=0$, whereas extending the second suggests $0^0=1$. Thus these rules do not give a consistent value at zero; in this treatment, $0^0$ remains undefined.

content.prompt: Write these expressions in terms of $\log_a x$, $\log_a y$ and $\log_a z$.

answer.worked:
By the product law,
$$\begin{align*}\log_a(yz)&=\log_a y+\log_a z\end{align*}$$

By the quotient law,
$$\begin{align*}\log_a\frac{z}{y}&=\log_a z-\log_a y\end{align*}$$

By the power law,
$$\begin{align*}\log_a y^4&=4\log_a y\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\log_a\frac{x^2y}{z^3}&=\log_a(x^2y)-\log_a z^3\\\log_a\frac{x^2y}{z^3}&=\log_a x^2+\log_a y-\log_a z^3\\\log_a\frac{x^2y}{z^3}&=2\log_a x+\log_a y-3\log_a z\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Prove by contradiction that $\log_2 3$ is irrational. Begin with the sentence, ‘Suppose by way of contradiction that $\log_2 3=\frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive whole numbers.’

answer.short: If $\log_2 3=\frac{a}{b}$ for positive whole numbers $a,b$, then $3^b=2^a$. This is impossible because $3^b$ is odd and $2^a$ is even. Hence $\log_2 3$ is irrational.
answer.worked:
Suppose by way of contradiction that $\log_2 3=\frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive whole numbers.

Multiplying by $b$ and using the logarithm power law gives
$$\begin{align*}b\log_2 3&=a\\\log_2(3^b)&=a.\end{align*}$$
In index form,
$$3^b=2^a.$$
But $3^b$ is odd and $2^a$ is even, since $a$ and $b$ are positive whole numbers. This is a contradiction. Therefore $\log_2 3$ is irrational.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Rewrite the formulae for $S$ and $D$ as quadratic equations in $2^x$. Hence express $x$ in terms of $S$, and in terms of $D$, in the case where $x>1$.

answer.short:
$(2^x)^2-2S(2^x)+1=0$ and $(2^x)^2-2D(2^x)-1=0$.

$x=\log_2\!\left(S+\sqrt{S^2-1}\right)$ and $x=\log_2\!\left(D+\sqrt{D^2+1}\right)$.

Substitute $u=2^x$ and select the roots consistent with $u>2$.
answer.worked:
Let $u=2^x$. Since $x>1$, $u>2$.

$$\begin{align*}2S&=u+\frac{1}{u}\\2Su&=u^2+1\\u^2-2Su+1&=0\end{align*}$$

Thus the quadratic in $2^x$ is $(2^x)^2-2S(2^x)+1=0$.

$$\begin{align*}u&=\frac{2S\pm\sqrt{4S^2-4}}{2}\\u&=S\pm\sqrt{S^2-1}\end{align*}$$

Here $S>1$. The two roots are positive with product $1$, so the smaller root is less than $1$. Since $u>2$, choose the larger root.

$$\begin{align*}2^x&=S+\sqrt{S^2-1}\\x&=\log_2\!\left(S+\sqrt{S^2-1}\right)\end{align*}$$

Similarly,

$$\begin{align*}2D&=u-\frac{1}{u}\\2Du&=u^2-1\\u^2-2Du-1&=0\end{align*}$$

Thus the quadratic in $2^x$ is $(2^x)^2-2D(2^x)-1=0$.

$$\begin{align*}u&=\frac{2D\pm\sqrt{4D^2+4}}{2}\\u&=D\pm\sqrt{D^2+1}\end{align*}$$

Since $\sqrt{D^2+1}>|D|$, the minus root is negative and cannot equal $2^x$.

$$\begin{align*}2^x&=D+\sqrt{D^2+1}\\x&=\log_2\!\left(D+\sqrt{D^2+1}\right)\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$\frac{1+y}{1-y}=\frac{S+D}{S-D}=2^{2x}$, so $x=\frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1+y}{1-y}$.

Use the sum and difference from part a, then take logarithms base $2$.
answer.worked:
Since $S=\frac{1}{2}(2^x+2^{-x})>0$, $y=D/S$ is defined. From part a, $S+D>0$ and $S-D>0$, so $-1<y<1$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{1+y}{1-y}&=\frac{1+D/S}{1-D/S}\\\frac{1+y}{1-y}&=\frac{S+D}{S-D}\\\frac{1+y}{1-y}&=\frac{2^x}{2^{-x}}\\\frac{1+y}{1-y}&=2^{2x}\end{align*}$$

Taking logarithms base $2$,

$$\begin{align*}\log_2\frac{1+y}{1-y}&=2x\\x&=\frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1+y}{1-y}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Use the change-of-base formula to show that

answer.short:
$\log_{1/3}x=\dfrac{\log_3x}{-1}=-\log_3x$.

All three curves decrease, with domain $x>0$, range $\mathbb R$ and vertical asymptote $x=0$. The first two cross at $(1,0)$; the third crosses at $(\tfrac12,0)$. See the shared sketch.
answer.worked:
For $x>0$,
$$\begin{align*}\log_{1/3}x&=\frac{\log_3x}{\log_3(1/3)}\\\log_{1/3}x&=\frac{\log_3x}{\log_3(3^{-1})}\\\log_{1/3}x&=\frac{\log_3x}{-1}\\\log_{1/3}x&=-\log_3x.\end{align*}$$
Reflect $y=\log_3x$ in the $x$-axis. The resulting curve $y=\log_{1/3}x$ passes through $(\tfrac13,1)$, $(1,0)$ and $(3,-1)$.

Dilate this curve vertically by factor $2$ to obtain $y=2\log_{1/3}x$, passing through $(\tfrac13,2)$, $(1,0)$ and $(3,-2)$.

Dilate the original curve horizontally by factor $\tfrac12$ to obtain $y=\log_{1/3}(2x)$, passing through $(\tfrac16,1)$, $(\tfrac12,0)$ and $(\tfrac32,-1)$.

Draw all three decreasing curves on the same axes. Each approaches $+\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ and $-\infty$ as $x\to\infty$; the $y$-axis is their common vertical asymptote.

answer.worked:
A horizontal dilation of factor $\tfrac12$ replaces $x$ by $2x$, giving $y=\log_5(2x)$. Reflection in the $y$-axis then replaces $x$ by $-x$, giving $y=\log_5(-2x)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}3^{x+4}&=3^4\times3^x\\3^{x+4}&=81\times3^x\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Dilate horizontally by factor $\frac14$ from the $y$-axis; alternatively, translate up 2 units.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\log_2(4x)&=\log_2 4+\log_2 x\\\log_2(4x)&=2+\log_2 x\end{align*}$$
Replacing $x$ by $4x=x/(1/4)$ gives a horizontal dilation by factor $\frac14$ from the $y$-axis. The equivalent rule $y=\log_2 x+2$ gives a translation up 2 units.

answer.short: Dilate horizontally by factor $\frac17$ from the $y$-axis; alternatively, translate up $\log_2 7$ units.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\log_2(7x)&=\log_2 7+\log_2 x\end{align*}$$
Replacing $x$ by $7x=x/(1/7)$ gives a horizontal dilation by factor $\frac17$ from the $y$-axis. The equivalent sum gives a translation up $\log_2 7$ units.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Describe two different transformations that send $y=6\times5^x$ to $y=5^x$.

answer.short: Dilate vertically by factor $\frac16$ from the $x$-axis; alternatively, translate right $\log_5 6$ units.
answer.worked:
Multiplying each ordinate by $\frac16$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\frac16(6\times5^x)&=5^x\end{align*}$$
For a horizontal translation, let $f(x)=6\times5^x$. Then
$$\begin{align*}f(x-\log_5 6)&=6\times5^{x-\log_5 6}\\f(x-\log_5 6)&=\frac{6\times5^x}{5^{\log_5 6}}\\f(x-\log_5 6)&=5^x\end{align*}$$
Thus translating right $\log_5 6$ units also gives the required graph.

answer.short:
The intersections lie strictly between $P=(\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$ and $Q=(\tfrac32,\tfrac12)$ on the line $y=2-x$. Hence $AB<PQ=\sqrt2$.

Use reflection in $y=x$ to obtain the second intersection from the first.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be the intersection with $y=2^x$. At $x=\tfrac12$, the exponential has height $\sqrt2<\tfrac32$, while the line has height $\tfrac32$. At $x=1$, the exponential has height $2>1$, the height of the line. Since the exponential increases and the line decreases, their intersection satisfies $\tfrac12<x_A<1$.

The two curves are reflections in $y=x$, and reflection in $y=x$ leaves the line $x+y=2$ unchanged. Thus $B$ is the reflection of $A$, so $1<x_B<\tfrac32$. Both intersections therefore lie strictly inside the segment joining $P=(\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$ to $Q=(\tfrac32,\tfrac12)$.

$$\begin{align*}PQ&=\sqrt{\left(\tfrac32-\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12-\tfrac32\right)^2}\\PQ&=\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $AB<\sqrt2$.

content.prompt: The population of a country is doubling every 30 years, and was $3\,000\,000$ at the last census.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why the population $P$ after another $n$ years is $P=3\,000\,000\times2^{n/30}$.

answer.short: There are $\frac{n}{30}$ thirty-year intervals in $n$ years, and the population doubles in each interval.
answer.worked:
The initial population is $3\,000\,000$. There are $\frac{n}{30}$ doubling periods in $n$ years, so the initial population is multiplied by $2^{n/30}$:

$$P=3\,000\,000\times2^{n/30}.$$

$$\begin{align*}P&=3\,000\,000\times2^{100/30}\\P&=3\,000\,000\times2^{10/3}\\P&\approx30\,238\,105.\end{align*}$$

To the nearest million, the population is $30\,000\,000$ people.

children.label: c
children.prompt: By substituting into the equation, find (nearest year) when the population will be:

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}60\,000\,000&=3\,000\,000\times2^{n/30}\\2^{n/30}&=20\\\frac{n}{30}&=\log_2 20\\n&=30\frac{\log_{10}20}{\log_{10}2}\\n&\approx129.6578.\end{align*}$$

To the nearest year, the population reaches $60\,000\,000$ after 130 years.

$$\begin{align*}\log_{10}P&=\log_{10}\bigl(100(1.05)^n\bigr)\\\log_{10}P&=\log_{10}100+\log_{10}(1.05)^n\\\log_{10}P&=2+n\log_{10}(1.05)\end{align*}$$
This has the form $y=mn+c$, where $y=\log_{10}P$, $m=\log_{10}(1.05)$ and $c=2$. Thus the second graph is a straight line with positive gradient and vertical intercept $2$.

content.prompt: [Moore’s law] Gordon Moore predicted in 1965 that over the next few decades, the number of transistors within a computer chip would very roughly double every two years — this is called Moore’s Law. Let $D_0$ be the density in 1975.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why the density $D$ after $n$ more years is predicted to be $D=D_0 2^{n/2}$.

answer.short: There are $n/2$ two-year periods in $n$ years, and the density doubles in each period.
answer.worked: There are $n/2$ two-year periods in $n$ years. Each period multiplies the initial density $D_0$ by $2$, so $$D=D_0 2^{n/2}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What was the predicted density for 2015?

children.label: c
children.prompt: Substitute into the formula to find, correct to the nearest year, the prediction of the year when the density increases by a factor of $10\,000\,000$.

answer.short:
2022.

Solve $2^{n/2}=10^7$ using logarithms, then add the elapsed time to 1975.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}10^7D_0&=D_0 2^{n/2}\\2^{n/2}&=10^7\\\frac n2&=\log_2(10^7)\\n&=\frac{2\log_{10}(10^7)}{\log_{10}2}\\n&\approx46.506993\end{align*}$$ The predicted calendar year is $1975+46.506993\approx2022$, to the nearest year.

content.prompt: [Newton’s law of cooling] A container of water, originally just below boiling point at $96^\circ\mathrm{C}$, is placed in a fridge whose temperature is $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The container is known to cool in such a way that its temperature halves every 20 minutes.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why the temperature $T^\circ\mathrm{C}$ after $n$ hours in the fridge is given by the function $T=96\times\left(\frac12\right)^{3n}$.

answer.short: There are $3n$ periods of 20 minutes in $n$ hours. Starting at $96^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and halving each period gives $T=96\times\left(\frac12\right)^{3n}$.
answer.worked: In $n$ hours there are $60n$ minutes, so the number of 20-minute periods is $\frac{60n}{20}=3n$. The initial temperature is $96^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and each period multiplies it by $\frac12$, giving $T=96\times\left(\frac12\right)^{3n}$.

These correspond to $n=0,\frac13,\frac23,1,\frac43,\frac53,2$. Plot the points and join them with a smooth decreasing exponential curve. The vertical intercept is $(0,96)$ and the horizontal asymptote is $T=0$.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain a half-life exponent, calculate the remaining percentage and use negative time to determine the original-to-present mass ratio.

content.prompt: [Decay of Uranium-235] Uranium-235 is a naturally-occurring isotope of uranium. It is particularly important because it can be made to fission, when it releases vast amounts of energy in a nuclear power station or a nuclear bomb. It has a half-life of about 700 million years, which means that if you store a mass of uranium-235 for 700 million years, half of it will then have decayed into other elements.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Explain why the mass of uranium-235 in the Earth $n$ years after the present is given by
$$M=M_0\times\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{n}{700\,000\,000}},$$
where $M_0$ is the mass in the Earth now.

answer.short: There are $\dfrac{n}{700\,000\,000}$ half-lives in $n$ years, and the mass is multiplied by $\dfrac12$ each half-life.
answer.worked:
There are $\dfrac{n}{700\,000\,000}$ periods of 700 million years in $n$ years. Starting with mass $M_0$ and multiplying by $\dfrac12$ for each period gives
$$M=M_0\times\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{n}{700\,000\,000}}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The Andromeda Galaxy will collide with our Milky Way galaxy in about 4 billion years. What percentage of the present uranium-235 will still be present in the Earth? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old. How many times as much uranium-235 was present in the Earth when it was formed? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$86.14$ times as much.

Use $n=-4.5$ billion years to calculate the original mass relative to the present mass.
answer.worked:
At the Earth's formation, $n=-4\,500\,000\,000$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{M}{M_0}&=\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{-4\,500\,000\,000}{700\,000\,000}}\\\frac{M}{M_0}&=\left(\frac12\right)^{-45/7}\\\frac{M}{M_0}&=2^{45/7}\\\frac{M}{M_0}&\approx86.14\end{align*}$$
There was about $86.14$ times as much uranium-235.

content.prompt:
[Decibels] Noise intensity $I$ is measured in units of watts per square metre $(\mathrm{W/m^2})$. The more common (absolute) decibel scale for noise intensity uses a reference level of $I_r=10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$, which is the auditory threshold of someone with perfect hearing. The (absolute) decibel level $n$ of noise with intensity $I$ is then defined as the ratio
$$n=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{I}{I_r}\right)\ \mathrm{dB}.$$
(One decibel is one-tenth of a bel, which explains the initial 10 in the formula.)

children.label: a
children.prompt: What decibel level corresponds to $4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ (nearest decibel)?

children.prompt: The sound level rises from $72\ \mathrm{dB}$ to $108\ \mathrm{dB}$ (rock concert level). By what multiple is the power increased? Give an exact expression and an approximation to the nearest whole number.

answer.worked:
For the same reference intensity, subtract the two decibel levels.
$$\begin{align*}108-72&=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right)\\\log_{10}\left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right)&=3.6\\\frac{I_2}{I_1}&=10^{3.6}\\\frac{I_2}{I_1}&\approx3981.\end{align*}$$
The power is increased by a factor of approximately 3981.

content.prompt: [The Richter scale] Earthquake strengths are usually reported on the Richter scale, which has several minor variants. They are all based on the log base 10 of the ‘shaking amplitude’ of the earthquake wave at some standardised distance from the epicentre. (An earthquake occurs kilometres underground — the epicentre is the point on the surface above the place where the earthquake occurs.)

children.label: a
children.prompt: An earthquake of strength 4.0–4.9 is classified as ‘light’, and will cause only minimal damage. An earthquake of strength 7.0 or above is classified as ‘major’, and will cause damage or total collapse to most buildings. What is the ratio of the shaking amplitudes of the smallest light quake and the smallest major quake?

answer.worked:
Let $A_L$ and $A_M$ be the shaking amplitudes of the smallest light and major quakes respectively.
$$\begin{align*}\log_{10}\left(\frac{A_M}{A_L}\right)&=7-4\\\frac{A_M}{A_L}&=10^3\\A_L:A_M&=1:1000\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The energy released by the quake is proportional to the $\frac{3}{2}$th power of the shaking amplitude. What is the ratio of the energies released by the quakes in part a?

children.label: c
children.prompt: An earthquake of magnitude 9.0 will cause total destruction. What are the ratios of the shaking amplitudes and the energies released of such an earthquake and the smallest light quake?

answer.short: Magnitude 9 : smallest light: shaking amplitudes $=100\,000:1$; energies $=10^{15/2}:1$, approximately $31\,622\,776.60:1$.
answer.worked:
Let $A_9,E_9$ refer to the magnitude 9 quake and $A_L,E_L$ to the smallest light quake.
$$\begin{align*}\log_{10}\left(\frac{A_9}{A_L}\right)&=9-4\\\frac{A_9}{A_L}&=10^5\\\frac{E_9}{E_L}&=\left(10^5\right)^{3/2}\\\frac{E_9}{E_L}&=10^{15/2}.\end{align*}$$
The amplitude ratio is $100\,000:1$ and the energy ratio is $10^{15/2}:1$.

inlines.text: [pH of a solution] The pH of a liquid is traditionally defined on a logarithmic scale as

is the hydrogen ion concentration in units of moles per litre (mol/L). It is not necessary to understand the units, except to know that the greater the concentration of hydrogen ions, the greater the acidity.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Rewrite the formula with $[\mathrm{H}^{+}]$ as the subject.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Pure water has a pH of about 7. What is its hydrogen ion concentration?

children.label: c
children.prompt: Lemon juice typically has a pH of about 2.0. What is its hydrogen ion concentration? How many times more acidic is it than pure water?

answer.short: About $10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol/L}$; about $100\,000$ times more acidic than pure water.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}[\mathrm{H}^{+}]&=10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol/L}\\\frac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{lemon}}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{water}}}&=\frac{10^{-2}}{10^{-7}}\\\frac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{lemon}}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{water}}}&=10^5\end{align*}$$
Lemon juice is about $100\,000$ times more acidic than pure water.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Sea water typically has a pH of about 8.1. What is its hydrogen ion concentration? How many times more alkaline (meaning ‘less acidic’) is it than pure water? Give answers to three significant figures.

answer.short: About $7.94\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{mol/L}$; about $12.6$ times less acidic than pure water.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}[\mathrm{H}^{+}]&=10^{-8.1}\ \mathrm{mol/L}\\{}[\mathrm{H}^{+}]&\approx7.94\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{mol/L}\\\frac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{water}}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{sea}}}&=\frac{10^{-7}}{10^{-8.1}}\\\frac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{water}}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{sea}}}&=10^{1.1}\\\frac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{water}}}{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]_{\text{sea}}}&\approx12.6\end{align*}$$
Sea water is about $12.6$ times less acidic than pure water, using the question’s meaning of ‘more alkaline’.

content.prompt: [Keyboard tuning] When a keyboard is tuned to modern concert pitch, the note A below middle C vibrates at $220\text{ Hz}$ (1 hertz is 1 vibration per second), and the note A′ above middle C vibrates at twice that frequency, which is $440\text{ Hz}$ (these names are not standard, but are convenient for this question). When modern *equal temperament* is used for the twelve semitones of the scale from A and A′, the frequency ratio of each semitone is $2^{1/12}$, so that on a logarithmic scale base 10, the log of all the semitones ratios is $\frac{1}{12}\log_{10}2$. Give non-exact numerical answers correct to two decimal places.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find, correct to two decimal places, the frequencies of C, C♯ and E, if the interval AC consists of three semitones, A C♯ of four semitones, and AE of seven semitones.

answer.worked:
After $n$ semitones, the frequency is $220(2^{1/12})^n=220\times2^{n/12}$ Hz.

$$\begin{align*}f_C&=220\times2^{3/12}\approx261.63\text{ Hz}\\f_{C\sharp}&=220\times2^{4/12}\approx277.18\text{ Hz}\\f_E&=220\times2^{7/12}\approx329.63\text{ Hz}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Unfortunately, intervals sound best when their ratios consist of small whole numbers, as most of them are in *meantone temperament*, the most common temperament from say 1500 to 1800. Using that temperament, find the frequencies of C, C♯ and E, if the interval AC is in the ratio $6:5$ (meaning frequency of C : frequency of A $=6:5$), A C♯ is in ratio $5:4$, and AE is in ratio $3:2$.

answer.short: C: $264\text{ Hz}$; C♯: $275\text{ Hz}$; E: $330\text{ Hz}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: When two frequencies close together are sounded together, there is an ugly *beat frequency*, which is the difference between the frequencies. Calculate the beat frequencies between the equal-tempered and meantone versions of C, C♯ and E.

answer.worked:
Use the absolute difference, keeping the equal-tempered frequencies unrounded.

$$\begin{align*}b_C&=\left|264-220\times2^{3/12}\right|\approx2.37\text{ Hz}\\b_{C\sharp}&=\left|275-220\times2^{4/12}\right|\approx2.18\text{ Hz}\\b_E&=\left|330-220\times2^{7/12}\right|\approx0.37\text{ Hz}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Meantone temperament is actually very complicated. Suppose that a careless tuner tuned A at $220\text{ Hz}$, then tuned three major thirds so that A C♯ was in ratio $5:4$, C♯ F was in ratio $5:4$, and F A′ was in ratio $5:4$. What would the resulting frequency of A′ be, and how would it beat with A′ tuned to $440\text{ Hz}$ on another instrument?

answer.short:
A′: $429.69\text{ Hz}$; beat frequency: $10.31\text{ Hz}$.

Multiply by $\frac54$ for each of the three major thirds, then take the frequency difference.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f_{A'}&=220\left(\frac54\right)^3\\f_{A'}&=\frac{6875}{16}=429.6875\text{ Hz}\\f_{A'}&\approx429.69\text{ Hz}\\b&=\left|440-\frac{6875}{16}\right|\\b&=\frac{165}{16}\approx10.31\text{ Hz}\end{align*}$$

The tuned A′ is lower than $440\text{ Hz}$ and produces about $10.31$ beats per second.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Meantone temperament gets its name from the fact that B between A and C♯ is tuned so that the log of its frequency is the mean of the logs of the frequencies of A and C♯ (B is two semitones above A, and two semitones below C♯). Find the meantone frequency of B, and the equal-temperament frequency of B.

answer.short:
Meantone: $245.97\text{ Hz}$; equal temperament: $246.94\text{ Hz}$.

The mean of the logarithms gives the geometric mean of the frequencies.
answer.worked:
Let $f_B$ be the meantone frequency of B, in Hz. From part b, the meantone frequency of C♯ is $275\text{ Hz}$.

$$\begin{align*}\log_{10}f_B&=\frac{\log_{10}220+\log_{10}275}{2}\\\log_{10}f_B&=\frac12\log_{10}(220\times275)\\\log_{10}f_B&=\log_{10}\sqrt{220\times275}\\f_B&=\sqrt{220\times275}=110\sqrt5\\f_B&\approx245.97\text{ Hz}\end{align*}$$

For equal temperament, B is two semitones above A:

$$\begin{align*}f_{B,\mathrm{equal}}&=220\times2^{2/12}\\f_{B,\mathrm{equal}}&\approx246.94\text{ Hz}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Write each expression in terms of $\log_a x$, $\log_a y$ and $\log_a z$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\log_a xyz&=\log_a x+\log_a(yz)\\\log_a xyz&=\log_a x+\log_a y+\log_a z\end{align*}$$

By the quotient law,
$$\log_a\frac{x}{y}=\log_a x-\log_a y.$$

By the power law,
$$\log_a x^3=3\log_a x.$$
$$\begin{align*}\log_a x^2y^5&=\log_a x^2+\log_a y^5\\\log_a x^2y^5&=2\log_a x+5\log_a y\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\log_a\frac{y^2}{xz^2}&=\log_a y^2-\log_a(xz^2)\\\log_a\frac{y^2}{xz^2}&=2\log_a y-\log_a x-\log_a z^2\\\log_a\frac{y^2}{xz^2}&=2\log_a y-\log_a x-2\log_a z\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Describe a sequence of transformations that will transform:
Then write down the domain and range of each transformed function, in both inequality or set notation and interval notation.

answer.short:
Dilate horizontally by factor $\frac13$, translate right $\frac73$ units, dilate vertically by factor $4$, then reflect in the $x$-axis.

Domain: $x>\frac73$, or $(\frac73,\infty)$. Range: $y\in\mathbb R$, or $(-\infty,\infty)$.
answer.worked:
Since $3x-7=3(x-\frac73)$, apply these transformations in order:

1. Dilate horizontally by factor $\frac13$, giving $y=\log_6(3x)$.
2. Translate right $\frac73$ units, giving $y=\log_6(3x-7)$.
3. Dilate vertically by factor $4$, giving $y=4\log_6(3x-7)$.
4. Reflect in the $x$-axis, giving $y=-4\log_6(3x-7)$.

The logarithm requires a positive argument:
$$\begin{align*}3x-7&>0\\3x&>7\\x&>\frac73.\end{align*}$$
Domain: $x>\frac73$, or $(\frac73,\infty)$.

A logarithm takes every real output value; the nonzero vertical dilation and reflection preserve this. Range: $y\in\mathbb R$, or $(-\infty,\infty)$.

answer.short:
Dilate horizontally by factor $2$, translate left $18$ units, reflect in the $x$-axis, then translate up $10$ units.

Domain: $x\in\mathbb R$, or $(-\infty,\infty)$. Range: $y<10$, or $(-\infty,10)$.
answer.worked:
Since $\frac12x+9=\frac12(x+18)$, apply these transformations in order:

1. Dilate horizontally by factor $2$, giving $y=6^{x/2}$.
2. Translate left $18$ units, giving $y=6^{(x+18)/2}=6^{x/2+9}$.
3. Reflect in the $x$-axis, giving $y=-6^{x/2+9}$.
4. Translate up $10$ units, giving $y=-6^{x/2+9}+10$.

The exponential is defined for every real input. Domain: $x\in\mathbb R$, or $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Since $6^{x/2+9}>0$, its negative is less than $0$, and adding $10$ gives every value below $10$. Range: $y<10$, or $(-\infty,10)$.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain a doubling model, evaluate it at whole and fractional doubling periods, and invert it using logarithms to determine elapsed time.

content.prompt: The number of bacteria growing in a Petri dish is doubling every four hours. Initially there were 100 bacteria.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why the formula for the population $P$ after $n$ hours is $P=100\times2^{\frac{n}{4}}$.

answer.short: There are $\frac{n}{4}$ four-hour periods in $n$ hours, each multiplying the initial population of 100 by 2.
answer.worked: The initial population is 100. There are $\frac{n}{4}$ four-hour periods in $n$ hours, and the population doubles during each period. Hence $P=100\times2^{\frac{n}{4}}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many bacteria are there after:

children.label: ii
children.prompt: 13 hours? Give your answer correct to two significant figures.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P&=100\times2^{13/4}\\P&=100\times2^{3.25}\\P&\approx951.3657\end{align*}$$
There are approximately 950 bacteria, correct to two significant figures.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Write the formula with $n$ as the subject.

answer.short:
$n=4\log_2\left(\frac{P}{100}\right)$.

Divide by 100, then convert from index form to logarithmic form.

children.label: d
children.prompt: How long, correct to the nearest hour, before there are $10\,000\,000$ bacteria?

answer.short:
66 hours.

Substitute the target population into $n=4\log_2(P/100)$ and use the change-of-base formula.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}n&=4\log_2\left(\frac{10\,000\,000}{100}\right)\\n&=4\log_2(100\,000)\\n&=\frac{4\log_{10}(100\,000)}{\log_{10}2}\\n&\approx66.4386\end{align*}$$

entries.description:
Index laws — combining powers with the same base
The first three index laws show how to combine powers when the base is fixed.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching introduction; reference evidence only.

entries.description:
Index laws — products, quotients and powers of powers
• To multiply powers with the same base, add the indices:
\(a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}\)
• To divide powers with the same base, subtract the indices:
\(a^m\div a^n=a^{m-n}\) (also written as \(\frac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}\))
• To raise a power to a power, multiply the indices:
\((a^m)^n=a^{mn}\)

• The power of a quotient is the quotient of the powers:

entries.sourceLabel: Negative and zero bases, and irrational indices
entries.description:
Negative numbers do not have square roots, so negative bases are impossible if a square root or fourth root or any even root is involved. For example, it may be reasonable to define (−64)^(1/3) = −4, but (−64)^(1/2) is undefined.
Powers of zero are only defined for positive indices x, in which case 0^x = 0 — for example, 0³ = 0. If the index x is negative, then 0^x is undefined, being the reciprocal of zero — for example, 0^(−3) is undefined. If the index is zero, then 0⁰ is also undefined.
We can only define irrational indices informally. To define 2^π, for example, take the sequence 3, 3.1, 3.14, 3.141, 3.1415, … of truncated decimals for π, then form the sequence of rational powers 2³, 2^3.1, 2^3.14, 2^3.141, 2^3.1415, …. Everything then works as expected.

entries.description:
Logarithmic and exponential functions are inverse functions
We have already seen that the functions log and 10ˣ are inverse functions. That is, when the two functions are applied to a number one after the other, in any order, the original number returns. Check, for example, using the buttons log and 10ˣ on your calculator, that
\(\log_{10}10^3=3\) and \(10^{\log_{10}3}=3\).
These relationships are true whatever the base of the logarithm, simply because of the definition of logarithms.
For example:
\(\log_2 2^6=6\), because 6 is the index, when \(2^6\) is written as a power of 2.
\(2^{\log_2 64}=64\), because \(\log_2 64\) is the index, when 64 is written as a power of 2.
The exponential and logarithmic functions to any base a are therefore called inverse functions.

entries.description:
The functions \(y=a^x\) and \(y=\log_a x\) are inverse functions
Let the base a be any positive real number not equal to 1. Then
• \(\log_a a^x=x\), for all real x, and
• \(a^{\log_a x}=x\), for all real \(x>0\).

entries.description: Three laws are particularly useful when working with logarithms:
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching introduction; no practice task.

entries.description:
The log of a product is the sum of the logs:
\(\log_a xy=\log_a x+\log_a y\)

The log of a quotient is the difference of the logs:
\(\log_a\frac{x}{y}=\log_a x-\log_a y\)

The log of a power is the multiple of the log:
\(\log_a x^n=n\log_a x\)

presentation.layout: Three vertically ordered bullet statements, each followed by its equation.

entries.exclusionReason: Standalone summary of logarithm laws; teaching reference only.

entries.description:
The simple reason for these three laws is that logarithms are indices, and these laws therefore mirror the index laws.
• When multiplying powers, add the indices.
• When dividing powers, subtract the indices.
• And when raising a power to a power, multiply the indices.

Here is a more formal proof.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation connecting logarithm laws to index laws; no practice task.

entries.description: To prove each law, show that \(a^{\mathrm{LHS}}=a^{\mathrm{RHS}}\), by using the second identity in the previous paragraph and the index laws for powers.

entries.description:

Finding approximations of logarithms to bases not on the calculator requires a formula that converts logarithms from one base to another.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching heading and introduction; reference evidence only.

entries.description:
The change-of-base formula
Let the bases a and b be positive real numbers not equal to 1.
• To write log base a in terms of log base b, use the formula
\(\log_a x=\frac{\log_b x}{\log_b a}.\)
Remember this as ‘the log of the number over the log of the base’.
• The calculator button log gives approximations for logs base 10, so to find logarithms to another base a, put b = 10 and use the formula
\(\log_a x=\frac{\log_{10}x}{\log_{10}a}.\)

entries.description:
To prove this formula, let \(y=\log_a x.\)
Then by the definition of logs, \(x=a^y\)
and taking logs base b of both sides, \(\log_b x=\log_b a^y.\)
Using the log laws, \(\log_b x=y\log_b a\)
and rearranging, \(y=\frac{\log_b x}{\log_b a},\) as required.

entries.description:
Writing 4^x = (2^x)^2, the equation becomes
(2^x)^2 − 7 × 2^x + 12 = 0.
Substitute u = 2^x,
u^2 − 7u + 12 = 0
(u − 4)(u − 3) = 0
u = 4 or 3,
and returning to x,
2^x = 4 or 2^x = 3
x = 2 or log_2 3.

entries.description:
Here are some of the properties of the two graphs:
• The two graphs are reflections of each other in the diagonal line y = x. This is because they are inverse functions of each other, so their tables of values are the same, except that the x-values and y-values have been swapped.
• For y = 2^x, the domain is all real x, also written as (−∞, ∞), and the range is y > 0, also written as (0, ∞). For y = log₂ x, the domain is x > 0, also written as (0, ∞), and the range is all real y, also written as (−∞, ∞).
• For y = 2^x, the x-axis is a horizontal asymptote — as x → −∞, y → 0. For y = log₂ x, the y-axis is a vertical asymptote — as x → 0⁺, y → −∞.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone graph properties; reference evidence only.

entries.description: The symbol x → 0⁺ here means, ‘As x approaches 0 from the right’. Elsewhere, we will use symbol x → 0⁻ to mean, ‘As x approaches 0 from the left’.

entries.description:
• As x → ∞, 2^x → ∞, and y = 2^x gets steeper all the time. As x → ∞, log₂ x → ∞, but y = log₂ x gets flatter all the time.
• The graph of y = 2^x is concave up, but y = log₂ x is concave down.
entries.exclusionReason: Continuation of standalone graph properties; reference evidence only.

entries.sourceLabel: 15 Exponential and logarithmic functions are inverse functions
entries.description:
Let the base a be any positive number not equal to 1.
• The functions y = a^x and y = log_a x are inverse functions, meaning that log_a(a^x) = x and a^(log_a x) = x.
• The graphs of y = a^x and y = log_a x are reflections of each other in the diagonal line y = x.
• The domains, the asymptotes, the steepness, and the concavity, of the two graphs are clearly seen from their graphs and this reflection property.
• We find base 2 logarithms by reading the graph of y = 2^x backwards. Input the number on the y-axis, go horizontally across to the graph of y = 2^x, go vertically down to the x-axis, and read the output off the x-axis.

entries.description:
Exponential functions with bases between 0 and 1 are reflections
In the introduction, the mould on the cheese was doubling every day, so its growth is proportional to the function y = 2^x. But the decay of radioactive element is specified by its half-life — for example, approximately half a sample of thorium-231 decays every day — so its decay is proportional to the exponential function y = (1/2)^x, whose base is between 0 and 1.

entries.description: The surprising result here is that the decay function y=(1/2)^x and the growth function y=2^x are reflections of each other in the y-axis, by successive applications of the index laws: y=(1/2)^x is the same as y=1/(2^x), which is the same as y=2^(-x). Because of this reflection, we can see immediately that the domains and ranges of the two functions are the same, and the x-axis is horizontal asymptote for both. But for y=(1/2)^x, the limiting behaviours as x→−∞ and as x→∞ are the reverse of y=2^x.

entries.description:
Dilations with negative factors
When a dilation with a negative factor is applied to an exponential or log function, it is usually better to regard it as the composition of a dilation with positive factor, and a reflection — in either order.
In particular, the behaviour of the transformed function near asymptotes and for large positive and negative values of x often reverses with a reflection, and the situation is usually far more straightforward to follow if it is done in two steps.
The following worked example should be enough to illustrate this point. There are four cases to cover, as is done in the challenging Question 12 in Exercise 9F.

[Decay of Uranium-235] Uranium-235 is a naturally-occurring isotope of uranium. It is particularly important because it can be made to fission, when it releases vast amounts of energy in a nuclear power station or a nuclear bomb. It has a half-life of about 700 million years, which means that if you store a mass of uranium-235 for 700 million years, half of it will then have decayed into other elements.
Explain why the mass of uranium-235 in the Earth n years after the present is given by M = M₀ × (1/2)^(n/700000000), where M₀ is the mass in the Earth now.
The Andromeda Galaxy will collide with our Milky Way galaxy in about 4 billion years. What percentage of the present uranium-235 will still be present in the Earth?

entries.description:
[Decibels] Noise intensity I is measured in units of watts per square metre (W/m²). The more common (absolute) decibel scale for noise intensity uses a reference level of I_r = 10⁻¹² W/m², which is the auditory threshold of someone with perfect hearing. The (absolute) decibel level n of noise with intensity I is then defined as the ratio
n = 10 log₁₀(I/I_r) dB.
(One decibel is one-tenth of a bel, which explains the initial 10 in the formula.)

[The Richter scale] Earthquake strengths are usually reported on the Richter scale, which has several minor variants. They are all based on the log base 10 of the ‘shaking amplitude’ of the earthquake wave at some standardised distance from the epicentre. (An earthquake occurs kilometres underground — the epicentre is the point on the surface above the place where the earthquake occurs.)

An earthquake of magnitude 9.0 will cause total destruction. What are the ratios of the shaking amplitudes and the energies released of such an earthquake and the smallest light quake?

[pH of a solution] The pH of a liquid is traditionally defined on a logarithmic scale as pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the hydrogen ion concentration in units of moles per litre (mol/L). It is not necessary to understand the units, except to know that the greater the concentration of hydrogen ions, the greater the acidity.

entries.description: [Keyboard tuning] When a keyboard is tuned to modern concert pitch, the note A below middle C vibrates at 220 Hz (1 hertz is 1 vibration per second), and the note A′ above middle C vibrates at twice that frequency, which is 440 Hz (these names are not standard, but are convenient for this question). When modern equal temperament is used for the twelve semitones of the scale from A and A′, the frequency ratio of each semitone is 2^{1/12}, so that on a logarithmic scale base 10, the log of all the semitones ratios is (1/12) log_{10} 2.

presentation.layout: Shared parent stem followed by five vertically stacked editable parts.

entries.description: Find, correct to two decimal places, the frequencies of C, C♯ and E, if the interval AC consists of three semitones, A C♯ of four semitones, and AE of seven semitones.

presentation.responseRequirements: Three frequencies in Hz, each correct to two decimal places.

entries.description: Unfortunately, intervals sound best when their ratios consist of small whole numbers, as most of them are in meantone temperament, the most common temperament from say 1500 to 1800. Using that temperament, find the frequencies of C, C♯ and E, if the interval AC is in the ratio 6 : 5 (meaning frequency of C : frequency of A = 6 : 5), A C♯ is in ratio 5 : 4, and AE is in ratio 3 : 2.

When two frequencies close together are sounded together, there is an ugly beat frequency, which is the difference between the frequencies. Calculate the beat frequencies between the equal-tempered and meantone versions of C, C♯ and E.

Meantone temperament is actually very complicated. Suppose that a careless tuner tuned A at 220 Hz, then tuned three major thirds so that A C♯ was in ratio 5 : 4, C♯ F was in ratio 5 : 4, and F A′ was in ratio 5 : 4. What would the resulting frequency of A′ be, and how would it beat with A′ tuned to 440 Hz on another instrument?

presentation.responseRequirements: Resulting frequency of A′ and its beat frequency against 440 Hz, with units.

entries.description: Meantone temperament gets its name from the fact that B between A and C♯ is tuned so that the log of its frequency is the mean of the logs of the frequencies of A and C♯ (B is two semitones above A, and two semitones below C♯). Find the meantone frequency of B, and the equal-temperament frequency of B.

presentation.responseRequirements: Two frequencies of B in Hz.
